Obtain CBC, metabolic profile, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing, and acute and convalescent Coxiella burnetii IgM, IgA, and IgG antibody titers. C
If the patient with Q fever has known or suspected valvular heart disease, obtain an echocardiogram. C
Treat acute Q fever in adults with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days. C
Treat children age 8 years or older or under age 8 years with high-risk criteria and acute Q fever with doxycycline 2.2 mg/kg per dose twice a day for 14 days (maximum 100 mg per dose). C

For children <8 years with mild or uncomplicated acute Q fever: doxycycline 2.2 mg/kg per dose twice a day for 5 days (maximum 100 mg per dose). If still febrile, give trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 4 to 20 mg/kg twice daily for 14 days (maximum dose 800 mg per dose). C

background.definition: Q fever is a zoonotic disease caused by C. burnetii, an intracellular gram-negative rod found worldwide. It frequently causes asymptomatic disease in humans, but can cause acute and chronic infection, including infective endocarditis.

list.listitem: Two cases reported per 10 million in the United States in 2004. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported 137 cases of acute Q fever and 39 cases of chronic Q fever in 2014.

Between 2008-2017, U.S. health departments reported 1,109 cases of acute Q fever and 272 chronic Q fever cases to the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System for a 10-year average annual incidence of 0.36 cases per million persons and 0.09 cases per million persons, respectively. The incidence of Q fever doubled from 2008 to 2017. Most cases (about 75%) occurred in men and annual incidence was highest among those aged 60-69 years. Interestingly, most (60%, n=380) patients with acute Q fever did not report exposure to animals in the 2 months before symptom onset and only 40% (n = 247) were employed in high-risk occupations.
Based on data from two national surveillance systems (2000-2011), the incidence rate was 0.38 cases per million persons per year.

Seroconversion rates among deployed US military populations were 7.2% for an incidence rate of 10.6 seroconversions per 1,000 person-months during an outbreak of Q fever in Iraq and 2.1% or 0.92 seroconversions per 1,000 person-months in southwest/central Asia.
The annual incidence of Q fever in France is reported as significantly higher at 17.5/100,000 in Cayenne and 1.9/100,000 in Marseille.

The seroprevalence of IgG antibodies to C. burnetii in the U.S. in the 2003 to 2004 National Health and Nutritional Examination Survey was 3.1% among more than 4,000 adults at least 20 years of age. Seroprevalence was higher in foreign-born adults, men, and adults with lower incomes.

Seroprevalence from Australia for 2012-2013 in a population sample of individuals aged 1-79 years was 5.6% (95% CI 4.5%-6.8%); higher among males (6.9% vs. 4.2% for females), but similar in metropolitan and non-metropolitan regions.

In the Danish National Birth Cohort of 100,418 pregnant women from 1996 to 2002, the proportion of women who were seropositive for C. burnetii was 47.2% in occupationally-exposed women, 32.2% in domestically-exposed women, and 4.8% in unexposed women.
Thirty percent to 60% of persons with preexisting valvular heart disease will develop Q fever endocarditis within 2 years of primary infection.
Cases of infection with C. burnetii have been reported in patients with culture-negative prosthetic joint arthritis.
C. burnetti has bioterrorism potential because of its air-borne transmission.
Exposure to milk, birth fluids, and excreta infected with C. burnetii.

C. burnetii is most often found in cattle, sheep, and goats, but is also found in other species of livestock, ticks, domesticated pets, and wildlife. Marine mammals also appear affected; in one study, 34.0% (73/215) of Pacific Northwest harbor seals had antibodies against C. burnetii. Organisms are excreted in milk, urine, and feces of infected animals.

Infection in humans usually occurs by inhalation of organisms from dust contaminated by dried birth fluids and excreta of infected animals. Authors of a systematic review found that infected sheep or goats, not cattle, were the likely source and airborne dispersal was the most prominent mechanism of infection; infection-risk occurred in rural areas within 5 km of the source but up to 18 km in high-wind conditions.
Other rare modes of infection include tick bites, ingestion of unpasteurized milk or dairy products, and human-to-human transmission.

The prevalence of C. burnetii in ticks collected in Africa varied from 2.9% to 14%, in Europe from 2.5% to 10.5%, and in the Middle East from 4.8% to 12.5% based on a meta-analysis of studies using data obtained by molecular detection of C. burnetii DNA in ticks.
Median incubation period, based on 23 studies, was 18 days and 95% of cases occurred between 7 and 32 days after exposure.

About 60% of infections are asymptomatic. Illness occurs within 2 to 3 weeks after exposure. However, there are different manifestations reported in different areas, suggesting different strains of C. Burnetii are responsible for infection.
There are two distinct antigenic phases of antibody responses—an antibody response to C. burnetii phase II antigen followed by a rising phase I IgG titer.
Polymorphisms in TLR1 (R80T), NOD2 (L1007fsX1), and MYD88 (-938C>A) are associated with risk for developing chronic Q fever.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Exposure to herd animals and their excreta

list.listitem: Take appropriate care of placenta and other birth products at facilities housing sheep and goats. C
Restrict access to facilities with potentially infected animals and consider vaccinating sheep and goats on farms open to the public. C
Avoid contact with C. burnetti-infected excreta and always use pasteurized milk products. C

An effective whole-cell vaccine is available in Australia (Q-Vax). Acellular C. burnetii vaccine is available in the United States for individuals dealing with pregnant goats or sheep (including veterinary students) or doing live bacteria research. Vaccine effectiveness appears high in these populations but effectiveness in the general population is uncertain. A
Postexposure prophylaxis (doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 1 week) should be started within 12 days after the known exposure. B

Routine population screening for Q fever is not recommended. C During a large Q fever outbreak in the Netherlands, routine C. burnetii screening starting at 20 weeks of gestation was not associated with a relevant reduction in obstetric complications (2.2% in women who were seropositive vs. 1.4% in the control group).

However, targeted screening among vulnerable populations in high-risk areas may be cost effective. In a study of 1,642 patients with specific underlying medical conditions (48% of those approached) from 13 general practices located in outbreak areas in the Netherlands, serum immunofluorescence assay showed that 289 (18%) had a previous C. burnetii infection (IgG II titer >1:64) and 9 patients were suspected of having chronic Q fever (IgG I y titer >1:512); 4 of whom were confirmed cases. The cost of screening was higher than anticipated, but the program was still deemed cost-effective.

Prevention of progression to endocarditis was achieved in patients with acute Q fever and valvulopathy by instituting 12-month treatment with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine in one cohort study. Interestingly, 31/72 patients with acute Q fever in this study had documented valvulpathy on transthoracic echocardiography.
Suspect Q fever in individuals with appropriate livestock or unpasteurized milk exposure history, fever or prolonged fever, and elevated transaminases. C
Obtain CBC, metabolic profile, PCR testing, and acute and convalescent C. burnetii IgM, IgA, and IgG antibody titers. C
If patient has known or suspected valvular heart disease, obtain an echocardiogram. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Clinically indistinguishable; obtain legionella serology and cold agglutinins

list.listitem: Use the Duke criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis, modification for Q fever (serology becomes a major criterion).

In patients with suspected Q fever, ask about occupations with animal contact, living within 10 miles of a farm that houses livestock (especially cattle, sheep and goats), travel, and having a family members or sexual partner with recent Q fever. In the 2000 to 2011 surveillance reports, however, most patients (61%) did not report exposure to cattle, goats, or sheep, suggesting that clinicians should consider Q fever even in the absence of livestock exposure. Similarly, in the 10-year incidence report cited above, 60% of persons with acute Q fever did not report exposure to animals in the 2 months before symptom onset and only 40% (n = 247) were employed in high-risk occupations.

Acute Q fever is characterized by abrupt onset of high fever (91%), fatigue, myalgias, headache (51%), sore throat, nonproductive cough, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, maculopapular or purpuric rash (11%), and chest pain. Onset is 2 to 3 weeks following exposure and fever duration is a median of 10 days (range 5-57 days).

Manifestations may be different in different regions. In a French report, while most patients had fever, pneumonia was present in more patients in Cayenne than Marseille (83% vs. 8%) while cardiovascular infections were less frequent in Cayenne than Marseille (7% vs. 17%).
Children typically have a milder disease course, but more gastrointestinal complaints (50%-80%) and more frequent skin rash (50%).
Thirty percent to 50% of patients with symptomatic infection develop pneumonia, and most have elevated transaminases or clinical hepatitis.
Features of Q fever pneumonia can’t be distinguished from other causes of community-acquired pneumonia.
Chronic disease is rare (<5%) and occurs within a few months to several years following acute infection.

Symptoms of chronic Q fever are nonspecific and include fatigue, fever, abdominal or chest pain, weight loss, and night sweats. Hepatosplenomegaly, arterial or pulmonary embolism or deep venous thrombosis, and valvular vegetations (12%) can be seen.

Q fever endocarditis: signs of heart failure or valvular dysfunction and vasculitic signs seen in other forms of infective endocarditis; clinical symptoms similar to acute Q fever. Endocarditis is the most common manifestation of chronic Q fever and is fatal if untreated.
Other manifestations of chronic Q fever are chronic hepatitis, chronic vascular infections, osteomyelitis, osteoarthritis, and chronic pulmonary infections.
Elevated transaminases up to 10 times normal (62%-85%), hyperbilirubinemia (25%), and thrombocytopenia (35%) are common.
Consider Q fever in cases with prolonged fever with elevated transaminases and normal CBC.
In acute Q fever, order PCR of whole blood or serum, IgM, IgA, and IgG antibodies to antiphase II antigens.

A definitive diagnosis requires a fourfold rise in phase II IgG antibody titer between acute and convalescent samples. Because this is a retrospective diagnosis, PCR, which can be positive very early after symptom onset, is now recommended. PCR becomes negative as the antibody titer increases and after administration of antibiotics. Antibiotic treatment does not appear to impede antibody response.

In chronic Q fever, order PCR, IgM, IgA, and IgG antibodies to antiphase I antigens. An IgG phase I titer ≥1:1024 at 6 months has the most favorable sensitivity and positive predictive value for the detection of chronic Q fever. PCR is performed because patients with chronic Q fever can experience a recurrent bacteremia similar to early acute infection.

A phase I IgG antibody titer >1:800 or a single positive blood culture for C. burnetii is a major criterion for infective endocarditis. PCR is positive in 33% to 64% of patients with Q fever endocarditis.
Cultures are not done commercially because of the high biohazard of organism. However, isolation of C. burnetii or IHC staining of the organism from a clinical specimen can also confirm diagnosis.

Abnormalities on chest X-ray are seen in most patients with acute Q fever; most commonly segmental or lobar consolidation. In a small case series, findings on high-resolution computed tomography were bilateral, peripheral areas of consolidation (all of 6 patients) and nodules with irregular contours and halos of ground-glass opacity (seen in 4 of 6 patients).

Obtain an echocardiogram for patients with acute Q fever and known or suspected valvular disease. Vegetations are seen in about 12% of patients with chronic Q fever endocarditis and may be difficult to see because of their small size and nodular shape. In one study of 85 patients with Q fever, cardiac valvulopathy was present in 39/66 for whom a screening echocardiogram was available. Echocardiography is not considered part of the routine work-up of patients with Q fever.

The presence of IgG anticardiolipin antibodies in patients with acute Q fever may be predictive of patients at higher risk for progression to endocarditis; these antibodies were significantly higher among patents with valvulopathy.
IgG anticardiolipin antibodies were associated with thrombosis during acute Q fever in a dose-dependent relationship in one study (area under the curve 0.83, 95%CI 0.73-0.93).

18F-FDG PET/CT can be helpful in the diagnosis of C burnetii focal, persistent infection. In one consecutive case series, use of this tool in 167 patients diagnosed with C burnetii infection resulted in 62.6% having their diagnosis changed and 38.7% had a previously unsuspected focus of infection discovered. There were 21 valvular foci, 34 vascular foci, 21 osteoarticular localizations and 9 pulmonary localizations.

Authors of a systematic review including 46 articles on use of PET scans for patients with chronic Q fever found the most frequent focus of infection was vascular, followed by musculoskeletal (infected prosthetic joints) then cardiac. Based on the retrospective and prospective studies, 394 had positive foci and 186 were negative for specific foci. Among the 53 individuals with follow-up scans, most (75.5%) showed improvement or resolution over an average of 8.9 months following initiation of treatment.

Suspect Q fever in patients with potential exposure to livestock or unpasteurized milk and high fever, fatigue, myalgias, headache, sore throat, nonproductive cough, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Agricultural workers are also at higher risk (OR 6.5; 95% CI, 1.7-25.3) compared with those in other occupations.
Obtain CBC, metabolic profile, PCR and acute and convalescent C. burnetii antibody titers.
If patient has known or suspected valvular heart disease, obtain echocardiogram.
If Q fever is confirmed, report the case to the CDC.
Treatment is not required for patients with asymptomatic Q fever or whose symptoms have resolved unless at high risk for chronic infection (e.g., valvular disease, immunocompromise).
Acute Q fever: doxycycline is the drug of choice for treatment of acute Q fever. See below for specific dosing recommendations from CDC for adults and children. C

Q fever endocarditis: give doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg orally three times daily for >18 months. The same drugs and doses are given for adults with non-cardiac organ disease, duration not specified by the CDC. C
For patients with noncardiac organ disease: give doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg orally three times daily. C
The CDC 2024 Clinical Guidance for Q fever can be found online. They recommend giving adults doxycycline 100 mg orally every 12 hours for 14 days for acute Q fever.

The CDC guidelines also recommend giving children age 8 years or older with acute Q fever or under age 8 years with high-risk criteria doxycycline 2.2 mg/kg per dose every 12 hours for 14 days (maximum 100 mg per dose). High-risk criteria include being hospitalized or with severe illness, preexisting heart valvulopathy or congenital heart disease, immunocompromise, or delayed Q fever diagnosis and experiencing illness for >14 days without symptom resolution.

Give children who are <8 years with mild or uncomplicated illness doxycycline 2.2 mg/kg per dose every 12 hours for 5 days (maximum 100 mg per dose). If the child remains febrile past 5 days of treatment, treat with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 4-20 mg/kg/24 hours (dose based on trimethoprim component) in equally divided doses every 12 hours (maximum: 320 mg trimethoprim per 24 hours).
Erythromycin is a less effective option.

Fluoroquinolones and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole are also effective but are the best options during pregnancy. The CDC guidelines recommend that pregnant people with acute Q fever receive trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 160 mg/800 mg every 12 hours throughout pregnancy, but not beyond 32 weeks of gestation. After that time, consult with infectious disease.
Chronic Q fever endocarditis: doxycycline 100 mg orally every 12 hours and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg every 8 hours for at least 18 months, or 24 months if prosthetic heart valves.
Hydroxychloroquine is contraindicated in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and those with retinal or visual field deficits.
For patients with non-cardiac organ disease, treatment is also doxycycline 100 mg orally every 12 hours plus hydroxychloroquine 200 mg orally every 8 hours.
Surgery may be required for damaged valves following C. burnetii endocarditis.
Consider cardiology referral if Q fever endocarditis is suspected.
Patients with Q fever do not need respiratory isolation or hospitalization if stable; they are not considered to be infectious to others.

Fatigue appears to be a long-term sequela of Q fever in up to 20%. No consensus has been reached on the pathogenesis of post-Q fever fatigue syndrome and cases are managed similarly to chronic fatigue syndrome. In a follow-up study of patients with acute Q fever, 40% of working patients reported sick leave for more than one month and 9% were still unable to function at pre-illness levels at one year or more due to fatigue or concentration difficulties. In a 3-arm RCT of 154 patients with severe fatigue lasting 6 months or more and significant disabilities following acute Q fever infection, fatigue was similar between doxycycline and placebo at the end of 26 weeks, but fatigue severity was significantly lower after cognitive behavioral therapy vs. placebo.

Q fever endocarditis is uncommon and can be difficult to diagnose. In a case series of 181 cases from 31 publications and four local cases, investigators found that most (72%) of patients had a history of contact with animals or travel and nearly all (98%) had positive serology. Surgery was performed in about half. Overall mortality was 17% and was higher for those with native valve endocarditis than with prosthetic valve endocarditis (12% and 3%, respectively). No patients treated with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine died.
In a systematic review and meta-analysis of non-endocarditis manifestations of chronic Q fever, vascular infections and osteomyelitis were the most common disease manifestations.
Although one study reported no association between Q fever and spontaneous abortion, the new US guideline lists miscarriage as a potential complication.
Sixty percent of infected individuals are asymptomatic; 2% to 5% of symptomatic individuals are hospitalized, and the fatality rate is 1% to 2%. B
The majority of acute Q fever cases resolve spontaneously within 2 to 3 weeks. C

The case fatality rate was reported at 2.0% (33 unique cases) and the hospitalization rate 62% based on 2000 to 2011 data. However, using single case-matched data from the CDC and US death certificate data, there was an estimated 129 fatal cases (95% CI, 62-1,250) during 2000 to 2011, so there is likely underreporting to the CDC.
In a large outbreak of Q fever in the Netherlands from 2007 to 2009, patients who died from acute Q fever were more likely to be male, older, and have underlying chronic conditions.
Mortality rate for individuals with Q fever endocarditis is 17% to 24%. B
Persistent infection develops in 1% to 5% of patients. In one large case series, 11/686 patients with Q fever developed chronic infection.

Persons who are most susceptible to chronic infection are those with valvular heart disease, a vascular graft, or an arterial aneurysm; those who are immunosuppressed; and pregnant patients. In a case-control study, independent risk factors for chronic Q fever were cardiac valvular disease (valvular surgery), vascular prosthesis, aneurysm, renal insufficiency, and older age.

Long-term (10 or more years) health outcomes reported from a cohort of 368 patients with Q-fever fatigue syndrome included low scores for health-related quality of life and high levels of fatigue, with post-exertional malaise complaints in nearly all patients. Young and middle-aged patients reported worse health outcomes compared with older patients.
For most patients with acute Q fever, follow-up serology and clinical assessment is performed in 6 months.
Based on one retrospective study, echocardiography and follow-up serological testing on all patients with acute Q fever are recommended by some experts.

Patients with cardiovascular risk factors at the time of acute infection and women infected during pregnancy should be monitored serologically and clinically at intervals of 3, 6, 12, 18, and 24 months for chronic infection.
Patients under treatment with hydroxychloroquine for chronic Q fever should undergo a baseline ophthalmic examination before treatment and every 6 months thereafter due to potential retinal toxicity.
The definition of a cured case of chronic Q fever is based on serologic testing defined as phase I IgG of ≤1:200. Some researchers use a titer of <1:800 to determine treatment duration.

Infection during pregnancy can cause miscarriage, prematurity, intrauterine growth retardation, or low birth weight. In a study from Scotland comparing 251 women who had experienced a miscarriage and a control group of 118 women who had not experienced miscarriage, the only 3 cases found to be positive for Q fever antibodies were from the group who had experienced miscarriage.

However, in a Danish cohort study of 397 pregnant women with occupational or domestic exposure to cattle or sheep and a random sample of 459 women with no animal exposure, women positive for antibodies against C. burnetii (indicating exposure) were not at higher risk for adverse pregnancy outcomes. Among the 10 women who seroconverted during pregnancy, all delivered live infants at term but two were small for gestational age.

In an Israeli study, where Q fever is endemic, seroprevalence among 386 pregnant women with preterm delivery was 4.1%. Similar percentages of neonates were small for gestational age (2/16 [12.5%] among seropositive women and 29/370 [7.8%] among seronegative women).
Tetracyclines are generally contraindicated in pregnant patients because of the risk of osseous malformations and the potential for hepatotoxicity in the mother.

Pregnant patients can be treated with fluoroquinolones or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (see treatment section above). Fluoroquinolones are pregnancy category C based on animal studies, but human studies suggest that they are safe in pregnancy.
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (160 mg/800 mg given every 12 hours throughout pregnancy, but not beyond 32 weeks gestation) is safe in pregnancy, except near term.
Postpartum patients with a serologic profile for chronic Q fever: give doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg orally every 8 hours for 12 months.
A course of doxycycline does not pose a substantial threat of tooth staining in children.
Dose of doxycycline in children is 2.2 mg/kg give every 12 hours (see treatment section above).

For children <8 years with mild or uncomplicated acute Q fever: doxycycline 2.2 mg/kg per dose every 12 hours for 5 days (maximum 100 mg per dose). If still febrile, give trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 4-20 mg/kg every 12 hours for 14 days (maximum dose 800 mg per dose).
C. burnetii is shed in breast milk, so this may be a risk to a nursing infant.
Chronic Q fever is rare in children, but when it occurs, osteomyelitis is the most common finding.
